title: Artificial Intelligence-Guided Cosolvent Design for High-Performance Perovskite/Silicon Tandem Solar Cells
summary: A retrieval‑augmented large language model screens >8000 solvents and identifies γ‑valerolactone (GVL) as a non‑toxic, high‑performance cosolvent for wide‑bandgap perovskites, establishing the first AI‑guided cosolvent strategy for perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells. GVL strongly coordinates FA+, delaying nucleation, promoting oriented micrometre‑scale grain growth, and enabling uniform ~1‑μm‑thick perovskite films on textured silicon with suppressed non‑radiative recombination and phase segregation. GVL-enabled devices achieve 23.3% (single-junction) and 32.5% (perovskite/silicon tandem) efficiencies, with excellent stability: T80 >4000 h (storage) and >1000 h (operational) for single-junction cells, demonstrating a scalable and sustainable solvent engineering route. A retrieval‑augmented large language model screens >8000 solvents and identifies γ‑valerolactone (GVL) as a non‑toxic, high‑performance cosolvent for wide‑bandgap perovskites, establishing the first AI‑guided cosolvent strategy for perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells. GVL strongly coordinates FA+, delaying nucleation, promoting oriented micrometre‑scale grain growth, and enabling uniform ~1‑μm‑thick perovskite films on textured silicon with suppressed non‑radiative recombination and phase segregation. GVL-enabled devices achieve 23.3% (single-junction) and 32.5% (perovskite/silicon tandem) efficiencies, with excellent stability: T80 >4000 h (storage) and >1000 h (operational) for single-junction cells, demonstrating a scalable and sustainable solvent engineering route. Realizing high-performance perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells requires precise control of wide-bandgap perovskite crystallization. Solvent engineering is the most direct lever for this task; yet, its intricate, multi-variable mechanisms defy intuition-driven design. Herein, we overcome this bottleneck by pioneering a retrieval-augmented large language model to screen > 8000 solvents, identifying γ-valerolactone (GVL) as a non-toxic, high-performance cosolvent. It is found that the GVL strongly coordinates FA+, thus precisely modulating crystallization kinetics, retarding nucleation, and promoting oriented, micrometer-scale grain growth. The resulting films exhibit not only superior crystallinity, reduced non-radiative recombination, but also improved scalability to large area and the tolerance to increased film thickness. Consequently, both the single-junction and tandem devices achieve efficiencies of 23.3% and 32.5%, respectively, along with excellent stability under moisture and illumination. This study establishes the first artificial intelligence (AI)-guided cosolvent strategy for 1-μm-thick perovskite layers in perovskite/silicon tandem architectures, underscoring the transformative role of generative AI in advancing high-performance photovoltaics.

screen.tldr: Retrieval-augmented LLM screens solvents to find a cosolvent that improves perovskite film formation, stability, and tandem solar-cell efficiency.
screen.transfer_note: AI-guided solvent screening and coordination-aware process optimization could help identify crystallization additives for organic crystal growth and polymorph control.

title: Interfacial Ionic Redistribution Induced by Sulfonate‐Anchored Dipotassium Salts Enables Efficient Buried Interface Engineering in Perovskite Solar Cells
summary: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) fabricated via two‐step sequential deposition commonly suffer from severe non‐radiative recombination at the buried electron transport layer/perovskite interface, where defect accumulation and unfavorable interfacial energetics limit device performance. Herein, we introduce a bifunctional methanedisulfonic acid dipotassium salt (DPMDS) interlayer to simultaneously regulate interfacial electrostatics and crystallization behavior. The sulfonate groups (–SO 3 − ) strongly coordinate with undercoordinated Sn 4+ sites on the SnO 2 surface, enabling effective passivation of oxygen‐vacancy‐related defects while inducing a positive interfacial dipole that optimizes energy‐level alignment and promotes charge extraction. Meanwhile, partial redistribution of K + ions into the adjacent perovskite layer modulates crystallization kinetics, leading to enlarged grains and reduced defect density. Benefiting from the synergistic effects of defect passivation, dipole‐induced electrostatic regulation, and crystallization control, the optimized PSC achieves a champion power conversion efficiency of 25.76% with an open‐circuit voltage of 1.184 V and retains over 80% of its initial efficiency after 3000 h of storage under dry ambient conditions. This work demonstrates an effective buried‐interface engineering strategy by integrating interfacial dipole formation with ionic regulation for high‐efficiency and stable perovskite solar cells.

screen.tldr: Sulfonate-anchored dipotassium interlayer passivates SnO2 defects, tunes interfacial dipoles, and alters perovskite crystallization to boost solar-cell efficiency and stability.
screen.transfer_note: Interfacial ion redistribution and crystallization control could inform additive engineering and nucleation tuning in solution-grown crystal searches.

title: Ligand exchange on nanocrystals: fundamental mechanisms, regulation of nanocrystal properties, self-assembly, and advanced applications
summary: Colloidal nanocrystals (NCs) represent essential building blocks for emerging next-generation technologies. However, long-chain organic ligands introduced during synthesis are electrically insulating, which creates substantial bottlenecks for charge transport in NC-based assemblies. In this review, we systematically summarize the well-established framework for NC surface coordination chemistry (X-, L-, and Z-type ligands) and sort out the existing mechanistic understandings regarding the thermodynamic equilibria and kinetic pathways that govern ligand displacement. Based on these fundamentals, we systematically evaluate ligand-exchange strategies including single-phase and two-phase solution methods, with an emphasis on their capabilities for atomic-level surface engineering. Importantly, we discuss how ligand engineering modulates interparticle interactions (e.g., van der Waals, electrostatic and magnetic forces) to direct the self-assembly of NCs into superlattices with strong interfacial electronic coupling. We further summarize the diverse applications of ligand-engineered NC assemblies in energy storage, catalysis and optoelectronics. To address the existing challenges regarding structural stability and scalable fabrication, we highlight future research directions, such as achieving uniform ligand exchange at the atomic scale, in situ characterization of exchange kinetics, and machine learning-assisted inverse design. Progress in these areas will facilitate the rational design of functional nanomaterials based on precisely tailored NCs.

screen.tldr: Review of ligand-exchange mechanisms on colloidal nanocrystals, emphasizing surface chemistry, self-assembly into superlattices, and applications in energy, catalysis, and optoelectronics.

title: Influence of Local Atomic Structure and Chemistry on Proton Conductivity and Electrical Leakage in Novel Proton-Conducting Oxides
summary: Electrolyte materials in solid-oxide electrolyzer cells (SOECs) require high, purely ionic conductivity to maximize their efficiency for hydrogen production. However, the most widely used electrolytes in proton-conducting SOECs exhibit non-negligible electrical leakage, usually arising from acceptor doping. As a result, it is desirable to identify and design materials that possess high protonic conductivity with minimal electrical leakage. Here, we use DFT calculations coupled with experimental analysis to examine candidate oxides to this end. We focus specifically on two promising hexagonal perovskite oxides, Ba 2 ScAlO 5 and Ba 7 Nb 4 MoO 20 . We explore how the structural and chemical motifs of these materials influence their proton conduction pathways: specifically, octahedrally coordinated cation-oxide layers have high proton conductivity, while tetrahedrally coordinated layers have limited conductivity. However, these tetrahedral layers contain what may be described as intrinsic oxygen vacancies, which may offer a pathway toward direct proton incorporation without the explicit need for acceptor doping. We nonetheless present results on the potential benefits of acceptor doping and elemental substitution, which is supported by experimental studies on doped materials. Our results provide physical insights into the ionic and electronic conductivity of novel proton conducting oxides. Additionally, we offer guidance for the design and development of superior proton-conducting electrolytes based on a holistic consideration of local atomic structure and chemistry. This work was performed under the auspices of the U.S. DOE by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory under Contract DE-AC52-07NA27344.

screen.tldr: DFT and experiments analyze proton transport and leakage in hexagonal perovskite oxides, identifying structural motifs that favor ionic conduction and doping strategies.

title: Role of First-Row d-Block Metals in Shaping the Properties of Nonstoichiometric SrTiO3.
summary: The A-site nonstoichiometry in doped ABO3 perovskites is typically introduced to tailor the materials' functional properties through defect engineering and to promote dopant exsolution. In this work, the redox behavior and electrical properties of 5 mol % Sr-deficient strontium titanate doped with the first-row d-block elements (Mn, Fe, Co, Ni) were investigated to elucidate the relationships between dopant characteristics and the resulting properties of the final materials. The materials were sintered at 1200 °C and 1400 °C to obtain samples with significantly different microstructures. The results indicate that although the B-O bond energy contributes to the overall physicochemical behavior of the investigated materials, the properties of SrTiO3-based systems are generally shaped by the nature of the dopant and, more specifically, by its intrinsic characteristics. In Fe- and Ni-doped materials, the key factor is the ability of these cations to be exsolved as metallic particles under reducing conditions. In Co-containing materials, the physicochemical behavior is strongly affected by the volatility of cobalt species at high temperatures. In contrast, Mn-doped systems are mainly influenced by temperature-dependent site preferences of Mn ions, which can occupy both the Sr and Ti sublattices.

screen.tldr: Experimental study of dopant-dependent redox and electrical behavior in nonstoichiometric SrTiO3, emphasizing exsolution, volatility, and site preference effects.

title: Engineering Proton-Conducting Ceramics: A Novel Study on Material Processing
summary: Protonic solid oxide electrolysis cells (P-SOECs) have emerged as a promising technology for efficient hydrogen production, primarily due to their low activation energy for proton conduction, which enables high water-splitting performance at intermediate temperatures. Central to the functionality and efficiency of P-SOECs are proton-conducting ceramic electrolytes, which play a decisive role in determining overall cell performance. Significant research efforts have been devoted to the development and optimization of high-performance protonic ceramics for use as electrolyte materials. Among the leading candidates are perovskite-based compounds such as Ba(Ce,Zr)O₃, doped with elements like Yttrium or Ytterbium. These materials have shown promise in balancing ionic transport, chemical resilience, and compatibility with high-temperature fabrication techniques. Nevertheless, concerns remain regarding the long-term stability of these materials, particularly following repeated thermal treatments during cell fabrication. High-temperature sintering, while essential for achieving desired densification and microstructural characteristics, can introduce challenges such as oversintering, nickel diffusion, and phase instability. In this study, we investigate how processing parameters influence the structural integrity of electrolyte materials and the electrochemical performance of P-SOECs, aiming to provide insights into optimizing manufacturing strategies for enhanced cell durability and efficiency.

screen.tldr: Studies processing effects on proton-conducting perovskite ceramics for solid oxide electrolysis cells, focusing on sintering, stability, and electrochemical performance.

title: Novel Organic–Inorganic Hybrid Cu(I)‐Based Metal Halides: Anti‐Thermal Quenching, Interconvertible Structure and Encryption Application
summary: Controllable structural switching and suppressed thermal quenching remain major challenges for luminescent metal halides. Herein, we report two novel interconvertible zero‐dimensional (0D) Cu(I)‐based hybrid halides, green‐emitting (5‐CTPP)CuBr 2 and orange‐emitting (5‐CTPP) 2 Cu 4 Br 6 (5‐CTPP = (5‐carboxypentyl)triphenylphosphonium, C 24 H 26 BrO 2 P), synthesized via similar protocols using identical reactants. Both compounds exhibit strong photoluminescence with high quantum yields of 98.0% for (5‐CTPP) 2 Cu 4 Br 6 and 46.3% for (5‐CTPP)CuBr 2 . Spectroscopic investigations and density functional theory (DFT) calculations confirm that the emissions originate from self‐trapped excitons (STEs). Notably, reversible structural transformation between the two phases can be readily triggered by methanol or thermal stimuli, accompanied by a dynamic photoluminescence color switch. Remarkably, both compounds display pronounced anti‐thermal quenching (ATQ) behavior within a specific temperature range, attributed to the thermal detrapping of excitons from shallow defect states. The combination of facile and controllable phase interconversion with distinctly separated excitation spectra highlights their promising potential for room‐temperature anti‐counterfeiting and encryption applications.

screen.tldr: Cu(I) hybrid halides show reversible phase switching, strong self-trapped-exciton emission, and anti-thermal quenching for luminescent encryption applications.

title: Porous Co-Fe-Ni Based MOF@MOF Nanoarchitectures as Bifunctional Electrocatalysts for Sustainable Overall Water Splitting
summary: Ongoing research aimed at fostering a sustainable future increasingly prioritizes minimizing environmental and climatic impacts. In this context, the utilization of fossil fuels is a primary contributor to environmental degradation because their combustion emits harmful gases that exacerbate global warming and air pollution. Among the various alternative energy sources, hydrogen gas production as a substitute for fossil fuels promises a secure and clean energy future. However, the mass production of hydrogen gas often relies on fossil fuels, thereby contributing to its carbon footprint. Water splitting has emerged as a method for generating hydrogen gas without emitting greenhouse gases. The use of highly efficient catalysts to decompose water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen gases is pivotal for future advancements. The high overpotential and sluggish kinetics of the two half-reactions involved in water splitting, namely the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER), necessitate the development of novel, efficient, and porous crystalline electrocatalysts. Given the high cost and limited availability of noble metal-based materials, such as Pt/C and IrO 2 /RuO 2 , it is imperative to explore alternative electrocatalysts derived from cost-effective metals for water splitting. The integration of inorganic and organic materials results in superior performance compared to individual materials, as it facilitates enhanced properties such as adjustable porous crystallinity, surface areas, and functionality. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), characterized by the coordination of metal ions and organic ligands, possess rich porous structures, exceptionally high specific surface areas, and numerous adjustable sites, making them applicable across various domains, including gas storage, sensors, catalysis, energy storage and conversion, gas separation, and drug release. Furthermore, MOF derivatives produced using MOFs as self-precursor/sacrificing templates to create metal sulfides, metal phosphides, metal oxides, carbon materials, and their composites with micro/nanostructures can retain the unique structural properties of MOF precursors. Nevertheless, the functionalization of MOFs with other MOF types remains a challenging and relatively unexplored area. The porous structure and metal ions within the MOFs serve as foundational elements for the self-assembly of homogeneous and/or heterogeneous MOFs, leading to the formation of hybrid structures. Consequently, ongoing research into MOF materials has culminated in the development of a novel family of MOF@MOF composites that utilize two or more MOF units. The investigation of novel MOF@MOF composite electrocatalysts for water splitting is driven by the use of inexpensive metals and the synthesis of electrocatalysts. In this work, a tri-transition metal-based composite was successfully synthesized on nickel foam. The resulting CoFeNi-C@NF electrocatalyst demonstrated high catalytic activity towards the HER and OER, requiring low overpotentials of 246 and 516 mV, respectively, to achieve a current density of 50 mA cm -2 . Additionally, this catalyst exhibited superior stability for the HER and OER, surpassing those of commercial Pt/C and RuO 2 catalysts. The CoFeNi-C@NF resulted in a full cell voltage of 1.69 V at the current density of 20 mA cm -2 . This performance is attributed to the advantageous porous crystalline nanoarchitecture, which provides a large surface area and abundant electroactive sites, thereby leading to remarkable electrocatalytic activity and stability under alkaline conditions. The achieved results excitedly suggested a novel catalyst for effectively producing hydrogen gas via the overall water-splitting process.

screen.tldr: MOF-on-MOF porous electrocatalyst design for water splitting, focusing on HER/OER performance rather than crystal structure prediction or polymorph discovery.
